Faust. Johann Wolfgang von Goethe's monumental dramatic poem, with Part I published in 1808 and Part II in 1832. It reimagines the medieval legend of the scholar who trades his soul to Mephistopheles for knowledge and power.

Faust is an aging scholar in Germany, disillusioned by the limits of book-learning. He summons Mephistopheles, the devil, and wagers his soul that the demon cannot find a moment of perfect fulfillment he wishes to prolong. The famous line, "Linger, O moment, thou art so fair," encapsulates the wager: Faust will lose only if he finds contentment to arrest time itself.

Rather than depicting damnation, Goethe's Faust explores the human drive to transcend limitation, to love, to create, and to act. Part I focuses on Faust's seduction of Gretchen, an innocent young woman. Her downfall and tragic end represent the destructive power of unchecked desire and the collision between Faust's ambition and moral limits.

Part II expands into cosmic allegory. Faust pursues ever grander projects—creating ideal beauty, founding a new nation—before finally achieving a vision of community benefit that earns him grace.

The work synthesizes German folk legend, medieval theology, ancient Greek drama, and Enlightenment skepticism. It creates a synthesis only Romanticism could contain: reason and emotion, ambition and morality, human and divine.

Mephistopheles is portrayed not as evil incarnate but as a cynical skeptic and facilitator—the principle of negation and ironic detachment—making the temptation psychologically nuanced rather than simply supernatural.

The Faustian bargain archetype, trading an eternal soul for temporal power, originates in folk legend but was crystallized by earlier dramatizations, particularly Christopher Marlowe's Doctor Faustus. Goethe transformed it into philosophy.

Faust became the cultural symbol of Western aspiration: the individual striving against limits, accepting moral ambiguity, seeking transcendence through creative action. It became a template for nineteenth-century heroic individualism.
